title: Job Curses the Day of His Birth
summary: After seven days of silence Job speaks, and his first words are a curse on the day he was born and the night he was conceived. He asks why he did not die at birth, pictures the grave as a place of rest where the weary and the oppressed are finally at peace, and asks why life is given to those who long for death. He ends in turmoil, saying that what he feared has come upon him and he has no rest.
story: The prologue ended with Job and his friends sitting in silence. Chapter 3 breaks that silence and changes the book's language from prose to poetry. The patient Job of chapters 1 and 2, who blessed the name of the LORD, now pours out a lament of astonishing bitterness. He does not curse God, as the accuser predicted, but he curses his own existence. This speech opens the dialogue that fills most of the book: Eliphaz will respond in chapters 4 and 5, and the argument between Job and his friends will run for many chapters. Everything they say is a reply to the anguish first voiced here.
historical:
The chapter's world is the same ancient Near East as the prologue. Laments over one's birth appear elsewhere in the Bible, most closely in Jeremiah 20:14-18, where the prophet curses the day he was born. Scholars have noted many similarities between the two passages and debate whether one draws on the other or both use a traditional form; since the date of Job is uncertain, the direction of influence cannot be settled.

The chapter mentions kings, counselors, and princes who built for themselves cities now in ruins and who filled their houses with gold and silver. The ancient Near East was full of such ruins, the remains of cities and palaces built by rulers long dead, and the image would have been familiar to any reader who had seen the mounds of abandoned cities.
cultural:
Ancient peoples believed words had power, and curses were serious acts. Job's curse on his birthday is not a spell he expects to work; the day is long past. It is a poetic way of wishing his life undone. He calls on those who curse the day, those prepared to rouse Leviathan. Leviathan was a sea monster that appears in several biblical texts as a figure of chaos (Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1; Job 41), and a similar creature named Lotan appears in texts from ancient Ugarit on the Syrian coast. The line is difficult: the Hebrew reads those who curse the day, but many scholars suggest a change of one vowel sound to read those who curse the sea (yam instead of yom), which would pair naturally with Leviathan, and translations differ. Either way, Job may be alluding to sorcerers thought to be able to curse days and stir up chaos, wishing the day of his birth to be swallowed by darkness.

The picture of the grave in verses 13-19 reflects the common Old Testament idea of Sheol, the place of the dead, where all go regardless of rank. There, Job says, kings and slaves, the small and the great, rest together. This is not a full doctrine of the afterlife but a lament; he imagines death as quiet rest because life has become unbearable.
literary: Job 3 is the first great poem of the book, and its movement is clear. Verses 3-10 are a curse, reversing the language of creation: where God said let there be light (Genesis 1:3), Job says may that day be darkness, and he calls on darkness, clouds, and gloom to swallow it. Verses 11-19 ask why, why did I not die at birth, and imagine the rest of the grave. Verses 20-26 widen the question to all who suffer, asking why light is given to the miserable. The poem uses Hebrew parallelism throughout, with each line echoed or developed by the next, and it piles up words for darkness. The word why marks the turn from curse to lament. The final verse is breathless, a list of what Job lacks: ease, quiet, and rest.

outline.t: A curse on the day of his birth
Why did I not die at birth?
Why is life given to the miserable?

doctrines.note: Job 3 gives voice to despair without rebuke from the text. Scripture includes this lament among its inspired words, showing that deep anguish can be spoken honestly in the presence of God.

Though Job doesn't address God directly here, his lament belongs to the tradition of complaint found in the Psalms. Later in the book he will turn his cry toward God, and at the end the LORD says Job spoke rightly of him.
Job's curse echoes the language of creation in reverse, calling light to become darkness. His pain is so great that he wishes his own small piece of creation undone.

words.note: Tsalmavet, deep darkness or shadow of death. The word appears in verse 5 and is the same word used in Psalm 23:4 for the dark valley. Scholars debate whether it is a compound meaning shadow of death or a word meaning deep darkness; either way, it names the darkest place imaginable.

Livyatan, Leviathan. A sea monster, often a symbol of chaos. Job calls on those who could rouse Leviathan to curse the day of his birth. The creature returns at the end of the book, when the LORD describes Leviathan at length as a creature under his own power (Job 41).

Nuach, to rest. Job imagines the grave as a place of rest (verses 13 and 17) and ends by saying he has no rest (verse 26). The longing for rest runs through Scripture, from the Sabbath to the rest Jesus offers the weary.

Sukh, to hedge in or fence. In verse 23 Job says God has hedged him in. The accuser used a closely related word in 1:10 for the protective hedge God had placed around Job. What was once protection now feels like a prison.

christ: Job's cry of why echoes throughout the Bible's laments and reaches its deepest point on the cross, where Jesus cried out, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Matthew 27:46), quoting Psalm 22. The link is not a prediction but a shared human anguish that Jesus took on himself. Job longs for the rest of the grave; Jesus, who went into the grave, offers a rest that death cannot give. Hebrews says Christ shared our humanity so that by his death he might “free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death” (Hebrews 2:15). Job's lament shows the depth of the human need that the gospel meets.

hard.q: Is it wrong for Job to wish he had never been born?
hard.a: Some readers think Job's lament crosses a line into despair and ingratitude toward God. Others note that Job does not curse God, that the Bible records similar words from Jeremiah (20:14-18), and that the LORD later says Job has spoken rightly of him (42:7), which suggests that honest lament is not condemned. The Psalms contain many complaints, some very dark, such as Psalm 88. Most interpreters conclude that Job's words are the cry of a man in agony and that the book includes them to show that faith can bring its darkest feelings into the open. At the same time, the book doesn't end here; Job's lament is the beginning of a longer struggle that leads him to meet God. For a reader who shares Job's feelings, the chapter gives words for pain without making those words the last word, and anyone thinking of ending their life should seek help from a trusted person, a pastor, or a crisis line right away.

questions: Job speaks his despair openly. Why do you think the Bible includes such dark words among its pages?
Job imagines death as rest. What kinds of weariness in your life or in others' lives might long for such rest, and where can real rest be found?
Job's first speech is lament, not argument. How might you listen to someone's lament before offering answers?
